scenario: WIBTA if I told my daughter to find a different hobby? | My daughter Ann (17) has been obsessed with building miniatures ever since she saw Hereditary a few months back. Since then, she has probably spent close to 500 dollars on miniature sets from Amazon, Hobby Lobby, and etsy. All of this money comes from her job at a local movie theatre, so I can't exactly cut her off. I can't explain why, but something about it drives me up the \*\*\*\*ing wall. Maybe it's because Toni Collette was so creepy? Maybe I just want to spend some quality time with my daughter instead of watching her waste her life in her bedroom. I hear my sister talk about dropping her daughter off at soccer, or how her son's the lead in the school play, and then think about how my daughter's upstairs building a tiny cottage with tweezers. She hasn't ever really shown interest in any hobbies before, so I thought it would be grateful that she's finally good at something, but mostly I'm just annoyed. I try to ask her if she'd like to go for a walk with me, or sign up for cheerleading, but she always says no. My husband thinks its sweet and has started letting her put them around the house and in his office at work. Every day, I drink coffee next to a 60 dollar miniature greenhouse, and think about when the last time I had a genuine conversation with my daughter that didn't revolve around the merits of craft glue versus hot glue was. ​ I know I'm probably the asshole, but would I be the asshole if I asked her to find another hobby that might help her in life? Like something she could stick on a resume?

Scenario:
WIBTA if I told my daughter to find a different hobby? | My daughter Ann (17) has been obsessed with building miniatures ever since she saw Hereditary a few months back. Since then, she has probably spent close to 500 dollars on miniature sets from Amazon, Hobby Lobby, and etsy. All of this money comes from her job at a local movie theatre, so I can't exactly cut her off. I can't explain why, but something about it drives me up the \*\*\*\*ing wall. Maybe it's because Toni Collette was so creepy? Maybe I just want to spend some quality time with my daughter instead of watching her waste her life in her bedroom. I hear my sister talk about dropping her daughter off at soccer, or how her son's the lead in the school play, and then think about how my daughter's upstairs building a tiny cottage with tweezers. She hasn't ever really shown interest in any hobbies before, so I thought it would be grateful that she's finally good at something, but mostly I'm just annoyed. Her grades are fine (Bs), her chores are always done, but mostly every second of her spare time is spent putting together miniatures. I try to ask her if she'd like to go for a walk with me, or sign up for cheerleading, but she always says no. My husband thinks its sweet and has started letting her put them around the house and in his office at work. Every day, I drink coffee next to a 60 dollar miniature greenhouse, and think about when the last time I had a genuine conversation with my daughter that didn't revolve around the merits of craft glue versus hot glue was. ​ I know I'm probably the asshole, but would I be the asshole if I asked her to find another hobby that might help her in life? Like something she could stick on a resume?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: I would rate this as 1, meaning YTA (You're The Asshole). The reason for this is that the daughter, Ann, has found a hobby that she's passionate about and good at, and it's not harming anyone or affecting her responsibilities (her grades are fine, and her chores are done). The fact that she's spending her own money on miniature sets and dedicating her spare time to it suggests that it brings her joy and fulfillment. The mother's annoyance seems to stem from her own personal biases and desires, rather than any genuine concern for Ann's well-being. She's comparing Ann's hobby to those of her sister's children, which is unfair and sets unrealistic expectations. She's also trying to dictate what Ann should be interested in, rather than supporting and encouraging her daughter's unique passions. Asking Ann to find another hobby that might be more "useful" or "resume-worthy" could be damaging to their relationship and stifle Ann's creativity and autonomy. It's essential to recognize and respect Ann's individuality and interests, even if they don't align with the mother's expectations. It's also worth noting that having a unique hobby like building miniatures can actually be a valuable asset in many ways, such as developing fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and attention to detail. Additionally, having a passion outside of academics or traditional extracurricular activities can help Ann develop a sense of identity and purpose. Overall, the mother should try to understand and support Ann's hobby, rather than trying to change her or dictate what she should be interested in. By doing so, she can strengthen their relationship and help Ann develop a positive and fulfilling passion.
